title: The Camphor Forest

pages.text:
*The Gatekeeper's Rules, Rule 12: When you are lost, follow the water down; when you are found, follow it up.*

The trail did not end so much as it forgot itself. One step on a flat stone, the next in a tangle of gnarled roots that gripped the mud like arthritic fingers. A-Bao stopped, his yellow raincoat bright against the dim green, and looked at Shu with the expression of a child who has been promised a straight road and given a maze instead.

"I don't see it," he said.

"Neither do I," said Shu. She pulled the folded paper from her pocket. It was Ouyang Min’s contour map, the one from the survey camp, printed on heavy stock that had survived the rain. She smoothed it against her knee, holding it up against the dappled light. The lines were thin and brown, winding across the page.

"Look here," Shu said, tapping a cluster of lines that were pressed so close together they looked like a single thick stripe. "Where the lines are crowded, the ground is steep. Where they are far apart, it is a gentle slope. We are standing on a ridge. The map says the ridge drops sharply to the west."

A-Bao squinted. "So we should go west?"

"No," said Shu. "We should follow the line of the ridge. It is the spine of the mountain. Keep it under your right hand."

She knelt in the soft earth and dragged a stick through the mud, drawing a series of concentric loops. "Imagine you are a bug," she said, pointing to the innermost loop. "You are at the top. If you crawl out to where the lines are close, you are on a cliff. If you crawl out to where they are wide, you are on a plateau. We want the middle. The shoulder."

A-Bao watched the stick carve the curves, then looked up at the canopy. "So the mountain has a skeleton," he said.

"Yes," said Shu. "And we are walking on the ribs."

Han, who had been checking his boots, looked up. "That is the most poetic thing I have ever heard from a person who owns a water level."

"Save it," Shu said, folding the map back into her pocket. "The mountain is not going anywhere. But the rain is still coming."
pages.image: Shu kneeling in the mud of a camphor forest, drawing concentric contour lines in the dirt with a stick, while A-Bao in a yellow raincoat watches intently, and Han in an orange life vest stands nearby holding a boot, with dense green trees in the background.

pages.text:
The ground tilted more sharply than the map had suggested, the forest floor giving way underfoot as the ferns grew thicker, their fronds uncurling into the path with the insistent grip of green fists. After ten minutes of climbing, the air grew cooler and wetter, the smell of the forest shifting from the sweet rot of leaves to the sharp, metallic scent of wet stone.

"I see water," Han said.

They crested a small rise and stopped. A stream cut across their path, not wide, but deep, the water dark and fast, tumbling over smooth, rounded rocks that glistened in the dim light. It was not a river, but it was certainly moving.

"Can we jump it?" A-Bao asked.

"No," said Shu.

"Can we go around?" Han asked.

Shu looked up the slope. The tree roots were thick and tangled, and the ground was steep. "It might take us an hour, or two. We have a deadline, Han. We are not here to hike. We are here to find a chest."

Han rolled his shoulders. He walked to the edge of the stream and lowered his pole into the water. The pole disappeared halfway before it touched the bottom. "Thirty centimeters," he said. "Maybe forty. The current is strong."

Shu pulled the rope from her pack. It was a thick, braided line, the kind used for the ferry, strong enough to hold a man and a duck. "Tie it to my waist," she said. "Then tie it to A-Bao. Then you."

"I am not tying myself to an eleven-year-old," Han said.

"You are tying yourself to a team," Shu corrected. "If one of us slips, the others hold. That is the rule. Water always finds its level, and it is never impatient about it. Neither should we be."

Han looked at the rope, then at the water. He grumbled something that sounded like a complaint about the weather, but he tied the knot. It was a bowline, tied tight and square. Shu watched his hands work, precise and quick.

"Ready?" she asked.

"Ready," Han said. He looked at A-Bao. "Don't fall in, little guy."

"I have a duckling," A-Bao said, with dignity. "He is better at swimming than me."
pages.image: Three figures standing at the edge of a fast-flowing mountain stream in a dark camphor forest, Shu holding a thick rope connected to Han and A-Bao, testing the water depth with a pole, the dark water rushing over smooth rocks.

pages.text:
The crossing was done in single file, one hand gripping the taut rope, the other testing the slick, cold stones for a foothold. The water was shockingly icy, pressing against their shins with a persistent, muscular force that reminded Shu of the pressure gauge on the mill’s intake valve. Han went first, his boots finding purchase with the sure, rhythmic confidence of a man who had spent his life on the Magpie, while Shu followed, her eyes fixed on the grey surface ahead, her mind calculating the distance to the bank. A-Bao brought up the rear, his yellow raincoat flapping in the wind, his face set in a mask of such intense concentration that he looked less like a child and more like a very small, very serious engineer.

When they were all on the far side, dripping and shivering, Shu untied the rope and coiled it with practiced efficiency. "Good work," she said, though her hands were still trembling slightly.

A-Bao sat down on a mossy log and immediately opened his lunch bag. "I think I am hungry," he said, as if the hunger had only just occurred to him.

"You have been hungry for an hour," Han said, wringing water from his shoe. "You just didn't have the words for it."

"I have a rice ball," A-Bao announced. He unwrapped it, revealing a perfect sphere of rice pressed tight inside plastic. He took a bite, chewed, and swallowed. Then he looked at the bag. It was empty.

"I ate it," he said. "All of it. In one go."

"That was your dinner," Shu said.

"I know," A-Bao said, brushing a crumb from his chin. "But it was delicious. And I was very hungry. It is a trade-off."

Shu exhaled, a sound that was half laugh, half relief. She took out a small flask of tea, warm from the pocket of her jacket, and poured a little into the cap. She passed it to Han, then to A-Bao. The tea was strong and bitter, tasting of camphor and deep earth, and it warmed them from the inside out, chasing the mountain chill from their bones.

"Dumpling needs a swim," A-Bao announced, lifting the bamboo basket. The duckling was pecking at the plastic, looking profoundly bored. Shu nodded. A-Bao found a shallow puddle near the base of a camphor tree, set the basket down, and let Dumpling out.

The duckling waddled into the water, splashing happily. It swam in a tight circle, dipping its head under, then up, preening its feathers with an air of supreme contentment. Then A-Bao gasped. "Dumpling has a leech."

A small, dark worm was attached to the duckling’s webbed foot, thick and wriggling with a slow, deliberate purpose.

"Salt," Shu said. She fished in her pocket and found a small packet. She sprinkled a pinch on the leech. It reacted instantly, curling up and sliding off the foot with a wet slip. A-Bao blew on the spot, then patted the duckling’s head with a gentle, reassuring stroke.

"That is a fact," he said. "Leeches hate salt. It is a fact I will remember."
pages.image: A-Bao in a yellow raincoat kneeling by a shallow puddle in the forest, carefully removing a small dark leech from a yellow duckling's foot, while Shu and Han watch, a flask of tea held between them, mossy rocks and ferns surrounding them.

pages.text:
The sun was sinking behind the camphor ridge, its light filtering through the high canopy in thin, golden shafts that felt more like dusty beams in an empty church than sunlight. The air grew cooler, and the mist began to rise from the valleys below, curling up the slope like steam from a kettle. Shu pulled her brass plumb bob from her pocket, the weight swinging gently on its cord before settling into a steady, vertical line.

"Look at the angle," she said. She held the bob up, letting it hang freely against the background of leaves. The shadow of the bob on the ground was long and thin, stretching out toward them. "The sun is low. We have maybe an hour of good light left."

Han looked up through the branches, his face half-lit by the fading gold. "It is dark up there," he said.

"Yes," Shu replied. "But the light is coming from the west. If we follow the water down, we will find the valley. If we follow the water up, we are climbing the peak."

They heard it then, a low, constant roar that seemed to come from everywhere at once. It was not the gentle babble of the stream they had crossed an hour ago, but a louder, deeper sound, a physical presence in the air that vibrated in their chests like a drum struck inside a hollow log.

"We are not alone," A-Bao said quietly, his eyes wide.

Shu shook her head. "No. We are just listening."

The roar grew louder as they walked, the sound wrapping around them, pressing against their ears with a steady, rhythmic pulse. The mist thickened, and the trees blurred into grey shapes, their bark indistinguishable from the fog. The path was gone again, replaced by a slope of loose gravel and tangled roots that grabbed at their boots with every step.

"I don't like this," Han said. His voice was tight, stripped of its usual easy confidence. "The map said the peak was to the north. We are going west."

"The map is a projection," Shu said, brushing a wet leaf from her shoulder. "It is a flat representation of a curved surface. It can be wrong. Or we are wrong. One of us is wrong."

"Or the mountain is moving," A-Bao suggested, with the serious tone of a boy who had learned that if everyone else is ignoring a fact, you have to say it.

Shu stopped. She listened to the roar. It was close now, so close she could feel the vibration in the soles of her boots, a steady thrumming that matched the beat of her own heart. "We are close to something," she said. "Something big. Something that makes noise."

Han looked at her, his expression wary. "A waterfall?"

"Maybe," Shu said. "Or a gate."
pages.image: Three figures standing in thick mist in a dark forest, looking toward a source of loud roaring sound, Shu holding a brass plumb bob up to the dim light, the trees blurred and grey, the atmosphere tense and mysterious.

pages.text:
The roar sharpened into a crash. The mist tore open like a wet curtain, and the rock face stood there, sheer and dark, bleeding a torrent of white water into a pool below. Spray rose high enough to catch the last slant of sunlight, bending it into a faint rainbow that arched over the churning water. The sound was no longer a presence; it was a physical weight, pressing against their eardrums with a steady, rhythmic pulse that vibrated in Shu’s sternum.

Half-hidden in the center of the rock face, just above the waterline, sat a small stone cairn. It was not a natural pile of scree. The stones were stacked with a meticulous care, each one balanced on the next with the precision of a gatekeeper setting a stone in the channel. It was a marker.

Shu walked forward, her green rubber boots finding no purchase on the slick moss. She reached the base of the cairn and looked up. Tied to the top stone was a strip of faded red cloth, tattered and old, its color washed out by years of rain and sun, but the shape of the knot was clear and distinct.

Shu recognized it instantly. It was a double bowline with a half-hitch, the exact same knot her grandfather used to secure the ferry’s mooring lines. It was a keeper’s knot, tied with the kind of muscle memory that lived in the hands rather than the head.

She reached out and touched the cloth. It was dry, which was strange considering the constant spray that misted the air around them. The cloth had been protected, or perhaps it had been tied there more recently than the weathered fabric suggested.

"This is a marker," she said, her voice cutting through the roar. "A trail marker. It means someone has been here. Recently."

Han leaned closer, squinting at the knot through the mist. "That is your grandfather’s knot," he said.

"Yes," Shu replied. "It is my family’s knot. It means the way is here. It means we are on the right path."

A-Bao looked at the waterfall, then at the cairn, and finally at his sister. "So the mountain is listening," he said. "And it is answering."

Shu looked at the red cloth, then at the roar of the water, feeling a quiet strength settle in her chest. They had climbed for hours, crossed the stream, and shared their tea. And now they had found the marker.

"The way is here," she said. "We keep climbing."
pages.image: A small stone cairn with a faded red cloth tied to the top, standing before a large, roaring waterfall in a misty forest, Shu reaching out to touch the cloth, Han and A-Bao standing behind her, the spray creating a rainbow in the dim light.

words: a line on a map connecting points of equal elevation
circles or rings sharing a common center
twisted together to form a strong cord or rope
showing great attention to detail and care
a pile of stones used as a trail marker
